hints: Notice the question asks about fringe spacing $x$, the distance between adjacent bright fringes on the screen, not about how bright the fringes are.
Recall the two-slit fringe formula $x = \lambda D / a$, where $D$ is slits-to-screen distance and $a$ is distance between the two slits.
Check each change to see if it increases $\lambda$, increases $D$, or decreases $a$, because only those changes make $x$ larger.
walkthrough: Identify the useful quantities: fringe separation $x$ depends on wavelength $\lambda$ of the single-frequency light, slits-to-screen distance $D$, and slit separation $a$.
State the governing rule for two-slit interference: $x = \lambda D / a$.
Use proportional reasoning: $x$ increases if $\lambda$ increases, if $D$ increases, or if $a$ decreases.
Test the options: brightness changes amplitude only; larger $a$ decreases $x$; higher frequency means smaller $\lambda$ so smaller $x$.
Increasing the distance between the slits and the screen increases $D$ with $\lambda$ and $a$ fixed, so $x$ increases. This is option B.

options.A: Increasing brightness increases amplitude and intensity of the fringes but does not change wavelength $\lambda$, slit separation $a$ or screen distance $D$, so fringe spacing is unchanged.
options.B: Fringe spacing $x = \lambda D / a$ is directly proportional to $D$, so moving the screen further from the slits spreads the pattern out and increases $x$.
options.C: Fringe spacing is inversely proportional to slit separation $a$, so increasing $a$ makes the fringes even closer together.
options.D: Increasing frequency $f$ decreases wavelength $\lambda = c/f$, and since $x$ is proportional to $\lambda$ the fringe spacing decreases.
